column1:
Adding the April 2020 SLOOS lens makes the overall read more negative than the FOMC+FSR take alone. While the FOMC pledged ZLB policy, open-ended Treasury/MBS/CMBS purchases, and robust repo/ON RRP operations—and the FSR showed those backstops restored market functioning—the SLOOS indicates a sharp tightening in bank credit supply that will weigh on activity.

Key SLOOS signals:
- Widespread tightening of lending standards and terms across C&I (all firm sizes), with wider loan spreads and higher costs of credit lines; tighter LTVs and credit policies cited, largely due to COVID-19 and a weaker economic outlook. Inquiries rose and near-term C&I demand from larger firms picked up (liquidity needs), but on tighter terms.
- CRE and multifamily: tighter standards/terms and weaker demand.
- Consumer: tighter HELOC standards with demand roughly unchanged; residential mortgage standards mixed across categories with some signs of stronger demand in segments like QM jumbos but no broad easing.
- Overall, banks (including U.S. branches of foreign banks) reported reduced risk tolerance and higher premiums, reinforcing an adverse near-term credit backdrop.

Bottom line: The FSR’s improvement in market functioning tempers tail risks, but SLOOS shows bank intermediation becoming more restrictive just as the FOMC notes “considerable risks” and impaired credit flow. Netting these, the sentiment shifts modestly more negative than before.
